https://www.ynetnews.com/article/sygwhsm.text: The case involving the smuggling of weapons from Ukraine, which were seized in November 2025 in a truck at the border crossing between Moldova and Romania, continues to widen and may now involve a rabbi. According to reports in Moldovan and Russian media, based mainly on a court ruling published as part of the legal proceedings, the name of Rabbi Pinhas Zaltzman, who presents himself as the chief rabbi of Moldova, was mentioned several times in testimony and investigative materials. However, the ruling does not determine that Zaltzman committed any offense, and he strongly denies any connection to the case. The affair began in November 2025, when Romanian customs authorities stopped a truck that had arrived from Moldova carrying advanced weapons, including anti-tank and anti-aircraft systems, RPG launchers and drone parts. The driver said then that “the destination of the shipment is Israel,” raising questions. Now, after the publication of parts of the ruling in the case of one of the defendants, it has emerged that one of those involved, Alexei Piankovsky, claimed in his interrogation that Zaltzman had asked him to transfer equipment from Ukraine to Moldova and later to Israel. According to Piankovsky’s testimony, Zaltzman described the items as “leftovers” from humanitarian equipment or as medical equipment intended for repair, not as weapons. The ruling noted that in mobile phones seized as part of the investigation, investigators found conversations between some of the defendants and Zaltzman, as well as photos of weapons and photos from his phone. Here too, the document does not determine the meaning of the findings and does not attribute criminal responsibility to him. The spokesman for Moldova’s Prosecutor’s Office for Combating Organized Crime refused to confirm or deny whether Zaltzman has any status in the case, saying only that “the investigation continues against several people whose identities are not being disclosed at this stage.” Alongside the legal reports, sources in Moldova’s Jewish community claimed that Zaltzman himself has not been seen in the country for many months. According to them, his last visit was in October 2025, and he has not returned to Moldova since, including during Hanukkah, Purim and Passover. The same sources also claimed that the Jewish community recently appointed Rabbi Menachem Mendel Axelrod as chief rabbi of Moldova. Zaltzman himself rejected the claims outright, saying he remains the chief rabbi of Moldova. “This is an old affair, with which I have no connection whatsoever," he told ynet. "Among the people quoted in the article is a Jewish criminal who sometimes came to pray at the synagogue. The attempt to drag my name into the incident is ridiculous and has no connection to reality. As part of my activities in recent years, I have had the privilege of greatly assisting tens of thousands of Jews, whether refugees from Ukraine or any refugee who needed help, regardless of origin or background. “In this framework, I worked extensively in the field of assistance, without any compensation and in accordance with the law,” Zaltzman continued. “The attempt, from the beginning, to turn this activity of mine into an attempt to smuggle weapons is a cynical exploitation by marginal political elements within the Jewish community, in place of an open-door policy of assistance to every Jew. There are countless witnesses who can testify to that. I am sorry that such a marginal, biased and false publication is being echoed in the Israeli press. All my life I have acted according to the law and out of a sense of mission to save Jews, and I will continue to do so.” The case continues to be handled in courts in Moldova and Romania. Some of the defendants have been released from custody, one admitted to the charges against him and was sentenced to a suspended prison term, and the investigation into additional suspects is still ongoing. According to Moldova’s Jewish community, Zaltzman is not the chief rabbi and is attributing to himself a role that is not his. “He was never elected or appointed to this position by the authorized bodies. He has no mandate to represent the community. The role he attributed to himself does not correspond to a position that has been recognized or approved institutionally and does not reflect the administrative structure of the organization’s leadership,” according to a statement issued by the community. In November 2025, Romanian customs authorities arrested a Moldovan citizen who was transporting in his truck an arsenal of heavy weapons, including anti-aircraft missile systems, anti-tank rockets and components for suicide drones. The driver declared at the time that the shipment was bound for Israel, but the shipping details have raised many doubts among politicians in Moldova, who believe the weapons came from Ukraine as part of a global smuggling chain.

https://maritime-executive.com/corporate.text: news features Podcasts magazine newsletter Jobs advertise subscribe 179 Views Upgraded Baltic Container Terminal Handles Largest Vessel to Call at Gdynia Published Jul 27, 2026 7:17 PM by The Maritime Executive [By ICTSI] Baltic Container Terminal (BCT), International Container Terminal Services, Inc.’s (ICTSI) operation at the Port of Gdynia, Poland, successfully handled the inaugural call of MSC Venice – the largest and longest vessel to call at the Port of Gdynia. The 399-meter-long vessel with a capacity of 16,652 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) recently docked at BCT, demonstrating the port’s capability to service the largest container ships operating in the Baltic Sea. Piotr Gorze?ski, Port of Gdynia Authority management board president and chief executive officer, highlighted the recent developments in the port and how they paved the way for the milestone: “The maiden call of MSC Venice is a historic moment and a very tangible result of the investments that have transformed the capabilities of our ports in recent years. The deepening of port waters, the reconstruction of the Helskie Quay, and the expansion of Turning Basin No. 2 have created the conditions for the safe handling of the largest container vessels entering the Baltic Sea. This is an important step for the Port of Gdynia, BCT and the entire port and logistics sector in Gdynia.” On the other hand, Patrick Chan, BCT chief executive officer, said: “The arrival of MSC Venice is a defining moment for BCT and the Port of Gdynia. It validates the significant investments made by all stakeholders to accommodate the next generation of larger container ships and reinforces our position as a deep-water gateway port to support Poland’s economic growth.” The vessel’s arrival marks the completion of recent upgrades in BCT, which include the commissioning of new quay cranes and yard equipment—investments that have significantly expanded the terminal’s operational capabilities and capacity efficiently handle the largest container vessels in the Baltic Sea. The successful call is also a result of years of cooperation with and commitment from numerous partners – the Port of Gdynia Authority, the Maritime Office in Gdynia, the Polish Navy and all stakeholders involved in the development of the port. The products and services herein described in this press release are not endorsed by The Maritime Executive. The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » Our Shows » Music Time » Music Time: Fête de la Musique in Bucharest Music Time: Fête de la Musique in Bucharest The Romanian trio Lisière Collectif and the French artist and producer Leo Pol performed in Control Club on the first night of Bucharest’s Fête de la Musique this year Listen to RRI in English Ana-Maria Popescu , 28.06.2026, 17:46 This week we talk about Fête de la Musique, Music Day, an annual celebration of music in mid-June or around the summer solstice. In Bucharest this year Control Club and the French Institute in Romania organised two days of events that brought together artists from France and Romania. And since electronics, house, techno, DJ sets and the like are rarely featured in our series, I thought this particular area deserves some more exploring, so I had a chat with Bogdan Ardeleanu of the Romanian trio Lisière Collectif, and with the French artist and producer Leo Pol, both of whom performed in Control Club on the first night of Bucharest’sFête de la Musique. The project Lisière Collectif was born out of a shared passion for nature, memory and minimalism; it approaches simple and minimalist themes in a sound that blends elegant electronic textures with techno grooves, one of the members, Bogdan Ardeleanu, told me just before their set. The first Fête de la Musique night of 2026 was beautifully rounded off by Leo Pol, an artist that constantly pushes the boundaries of music genres and plays with house, trance, techno, hip-hop, pop and everything in between. With over 10 million streams for tracks like This Must Be Illegal and You Got The Funk, he quickly built an international reputation that brought him to venues and festivals such as Berghain / Panorama Bar, Printworks, DC-10, Shelter Amsterdam, Gazgolder, Exit Festival and Khidi. The launch of the Tigh Pop label in 2023 was the start of a new stage in Leo Pol’s career, with a project that pushes the boundaries of electronic music and combines eurodance, pop and techno influences, with a strong emphasis on vocals.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: 1:54 Visitors delighted to see Bayeux tapestry on display in the UK for the first time – video Bayeux tapestry Francophiles, Norman outfits and broken threads: visitors see Bayeux tapestry in UK for first time Visitors got a first glimpse of the medieval artefact after it went on display at the British Museum in London Rachel Hall Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.42 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 15.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n the day Bayeux tapestry tickets were released, Megan Stockwell was at the beach. She was so determined to lock down her spot, that she sat with her toes in the sand for an hour, waiting in the online queue. “The whole ticket buying experience felt like what other people would do to get Taylor Swift tickets. I was like, ‘oh God, am I, like, the geek version of this?’” she recalled. View image in fullscreen Megan Stockwell outside the British Museum. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Like any committed Swiftie, Stockwell felt confident the experience would be worth the hassle and cost. As a self-professed Francophile, she was fascinated by how the tapestry, which is temporarily housed at the British Museum until next July, tells the story of the Franco-British relationship through the Norman conquest, culminating in the battle of Hastings. “You just grow up learning so much about it – at primary school, in history studies. You’ve always got some mention of the Bayeux tapestry, the Normans, the fact there’s even three lions on the back of our pound coins comes from Normandy. “We’ve got such a close connection between French and British culture, our language and everything. This sort of feels like a visual representation of that,” she said. Stockwell’s dogged pursuit of tickets, fascination with the Franco-British relationship, and childhood memories of learning about the battle of Hastings, were experiences shared by many of the visitors on the exhibition’s opening day. Cydney, who lives in Texas, also drew inspiration from her experience queueing for concert tickets to secure a coveted opening day spot. She had woken up at 3am local time to join an online queue for an hour and half to secure them when they were released. Why the Bayeux tapestry and Franco-British relations are natural bedfellows Read more She anticipated it would be worth it: “It’s going to be life-changing, we’re so excited.” View image in fullscreen Cydney, who lives in Texas, said seeing the tapestry would be ‘life-changing’. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Cydney had studied history for her undergraduate degree. “So I just really am interested to see what a significant artefact would be and to see how this is basically where the history of England and the UK as we know it really all began. Seeing something so old is just incredible and honestly such an honour.” Her feelings were echoed by Adrian Harris, who was so moved to catch the exhibition that he signed up for British Museum membership purposely to gain early access to tickets. He ended up the second person through the doors on Thursday morning, after joining a “really jolly” queue at 9.30am. View image in fullscreen Adrian Harris. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian “It was incredible. It was very, very moving to walk down the steps and to see the length and breadth of it. And I think they’ve done it so well, the British Museum. It was very profound to see it,” he said, adding he had been especially thrilled to spy Westminster Abbey, where he works, on the cloth. He noted that although he was one of the first through the doors, he felt that 40 minutes was a restricted timeframe to see the 68-metre tapestry, though he observed that attendants were diligent in ushering people along. A number of ticket holders for the Bayeux tapestry at a special first viewing last weekend were reportedly turned away after other visitors took too long to view it. The French owners of the tapestry have issued strict orders on when lights must be turned off in order to preserve the work. Richard and Madeleine Abramson, who were in the first group alongside visitors dressed in Norman costumes, agreed that 40 minutes was a short time, but that it was being well policed. “They’re very clear at the beginning there’s a maximum time … they’re very carefully moving you on,” said Madeleine. However, the oversight did not dampen the pair’s enthusiasm. “It was pretty awe-inspiring,” said Richard. “It’s very well presented, it develops like a film. It’s got a story to tell: it starts quietly, then it gets more intrigue and then you get to the action and it builds up to the battle, which is quite violent.” Madeleine felt the tapestry loomed large for many former English schoolchildren. “Of all the history lessons you have, every child remembers 1066,” she said, adding that the fact the tapestry was woven by female embroiderers also resonated. “[That they] told this whole story is still phenomenal,” she said. View image in fullscreen Richard and Madeleine Abramson said the exhibition was ‘pretty awe-inspiring’. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Vivien and Karen had travelled from Hampshire to see the tapestry, also buoyed up by memories of their school days. “We learned about it at school. It’s something that’s always been in the back of your mind, then all of a sudden it’s here, so why not?” said Karen. Vivien practises needlework, and was especially excited to witness the craftsmanship up close. “I’ll be looking for the two broken threads,” she said. Denise Davies had bought two tickets for her husband John’s birthday. As a taxi driver who also runs black cab heritage tours of London, he was looking forward to expanding his historical knowledge. At £33 a peak-time ticket, the exhibition’s cost has attracted some criticism – but Denise felt it was worth it. “ I could go to Alton Towers and it would cost me an arm and a leg. This is something special. I would have paid whatever it was because we’re never going to see it again … it’s a tick on the bucket list, basically.” Explore more on these topics Bayeux tapestry France History Europe Museums features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Feeling Bayeux tapestry Fomo? https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/opinion-g.text: Melanie McDonagh Thu, September 10, 2026 at 10:43 AM UTC 1 There is one thing to bear in mind when considering the actions of the Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband , in imposing sanctions on Jewish settlements in the occupied territories and it is the stance of his mother, Marion, who died earlier this year. Marion Kozak was a Polish Jew who survived the Holocaust by taking refuge in a convent. She made her life here and, like her husband Ralph, was a social activist and campaigner for the causes she believed in. And one of those causes was a just settlement for Palestinians. She was one of the founding signatories of a group called Jews for Justice for Palestinians, which calls for an end to the Israeli occupation of recognised Palestinian territories. On the expanding Israeli settlements, against which the Government has announced sanctions, it says, “ Israel ’s declared motive for its offensives policy is to suppress expected terrorist attacks. However, the continued settlement expansion makes it clear that much of its motive is to expand settlements under cover of the war on Gaza.” It’s worth looking at the group’s website: its sentiments are of a piece with everything the Foreign Secretary has been saying about Britain’s current attitude towards Israel — or rather, towards the Israeli government. Miliband is his mother’s son. It’s also how many ordinary people, me included, feel about what’s going on in the occupied territories. What can’t be said often enough is that there is an absolute distinction between Israel, and indeed Jews, and the actions of the government of Benjamin Netanyahu . And there is a real difference between being anti the policies of that government and being antisemitic. As the Foreign Secretary said, “We all need to do more to tackle antisemitism, but I believe we can do that and stand up for British values”. British Jews under threat When Jews for Justice for Palestinians say, as they do, “Not in My Name”, they echo the sentiments of many British Jews. Don’t take it from me: I speak as an outsider. At a gathering outside the Israeli Embassy the other day I saw a plucky little group with placards saying Jews Against the Occupation. You see them at almost every pro-Palestinian demonstration. They may of course be a small minority of the Jewish community but they single-handedly give the lie to the notion that being Jewish is tantamount to being a supporter of the Netanyahu administration and its support for the settler violence in the West Bank . It is that strand of liberal Jewish identity that Miliband represents, as did his mother. These liberal Jews are not alone in feeling repugnance at the actions of the Israeli PM. David Abulafia, a conservative Cambridge don who died recently, was contemptuous about Netanyahu: “I regard him as a crook,” he told me. He was an example of the diversity of British Jews; his family was one of those who had always lived in Jerusalem, from long before the establishment of the state of Israel. One of the many tragedies of the present situation in the West Bank and Gaza is that it has increased antisemitic attacks by those Palestinian activists who cannot make the crucial distinction between being Jewish and supporting this particular Israeli government. That failure to distinguish between the Jewish community as a whole and the coalition behind the Israeli government is, to my mind, wicked. But the attacks unquestionably have escalated as the situation has worsened — and London’s Jewish community is justified in feeling under threat. Bid to see off two-state solution London Jews aren’t responsible for settlers in the West Bank attacking villages and attempting to deprive them of their homes, yet they are bearing the brunt of the indignation at what’s happening. The Chief Rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, a humane and intelligent man, has said that the imposition of sanctions marks a “dark day” for Britain’s Jews. Yet it’s not the sanctions which are causing anti-Jewish sentiment; it’s what’s happening in Israel. Sanctions are simply a reflection of the revulsion many British people feel at what’s going on. A spokesman for the Israeli government in London declared that the sanctions create a fertile ground for antisemitism to flourish. They have, he says, nothing to do with the situation on the ground but “everything to do with politics”, by which he probably means the Labour MPs whose majorities depend on Muslim votes. Sorry, but that’s the wrong way round. It’s the situation on the ground which aggravates antisemitism. And the actions of Jewish settlers in the West Bank are indeed tantamount to ethnic cleansing; even members of the Israeli military acknowledge as much and resent it. There are now hundreds of thousands of settlers in the occupied territories where they have no right to be. That’s the problem. As the Foreign Secretary has made clear, it’s a blatant bid to see off a two-state solution. We’re a long way from the kind of Israel politics that made possible the Oslo agreement, worse luck. In other words, Miliband isn’t the problem. Sanctions aren’t the problem. It’s what a godawful government in Israel is doing that’s the real problem. And until that problem is resolved, British Jews will — iniquitously — be blamed for the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu.
